cards.title: Treat all client-supplied data as untrusted input
cards.summary: Any value from URLs, form fields, headers or profile data must be escaped before insertion into HTML or JavaScript, because client data can never be trusted.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing any storefront feature that echoes user input — search terms, review text, profile names, wishlist labels, coupon codes, or URL parameters — back into the page.
steps: Assume every value originating from the browser (query string, form field, header, stored profile field) is suspect regardless of how mundane it looks.
Identify every place that value is inserted into HTML, an attribute, or inline JavaScript — each insertion point needs its own correct escaping.
Prefer the escaping mechanism built into your framework or templating language (e.g. ejs, Jade) over hand-rolled concatenation of HTML strings with user data.
Read the framework docs to find the safe insertion helper and the explicitly dangerous opt-out; treat the opt-out as requiring justification, not convenience.
For high-power attributes (src, href, style, event handlers), do not rely on generic escaping; validate the value separately (see related cards).
Log where untrusted data enters your stack so future features inherit the same discipline.
caveats: The source cites research (a WhiteHat Security report circa 2015-2016) that roughly half of sites had XSS issues; this is a historical statistic, not a current benchmark.
Framework behaviour and default escaping change over time — verify the current interface and defaults for whatever framework you use.

cards.title: Escape user data inside HTML element contexts
cards.summary: When inserting untrusted data between HTML tags, escape the left angle bracket, ampersand, and both quote characters to neutralize injected markup.
cards.use_when: Rendering user-supplied text into normal page regions such as review bodies, collection descriptions, order notes, or any block that is not a script, style, comment or tag name.
steps: Replace left angle brackets (<) with the HTML entity (<) so the browser shows the character instead of starting a tag.
Also replace ampersands (&) with the entity (&) — otherwise a user typing the literal sequence '<' would be rendered as a real '<' and could re-open an injection.
For attribute values, additionally convert both single and double quotes to their HTML entities, so it does not matter which quote character surrounds the attribute.
Do not apply HTML entity escaping to the whole page — that would show every legitimate tag as visible text; only escape the specific untrusted variables.
Where possible delegate this to your framework's safe-insertion helper, but understand what it does so you can audit it.
caveats: This rule covers ordinary element text and quoted attribute values only; script and style blocks have completely different rules.
Escaping entities inside a script block does not work because the JavaScript parser does not understand HTML entities.
Over-escaping is generally harmless to display (any character can be turned into an entity), but it breaks contexts where the parser expects raw characters.

cards.title: Always quote HTML attribute values you build
cards.summary: Unquoted attributes let browsers treat many characters as ending the value, so never build storefront attributes without surrounding quotes.
cards.use_when: Generating HTML snippets for product images, alt text, srcsets, data attributes, or any element whose attribute values include dynamic store data.
steps: Always wrap dynamic attribute values in quotes in your templates; do not emit attributes like alt=userText with no quotes.
Recognise that an unquoted value cannot safely contain a space, and browsers also treat many other characters as ending the value, not just spaces.
Treat unquoted attributes as effectively impossible to escape correctly, because you would need to block a long and browser-dependent list of characters.
When reviewing templates or generated markup, flag any attribute whose value is unquoted and dynamic.
Rely on the framework's templating, which quotes attributes for you, rather than manual string concatenation.
caveats: Historically browsers disagreed on which characters terminated unquoted values; behaviour is more standardised now but still a poor practice.
This is defence-in-depth: quoting alone does not make high-power attributes safe.

cards.title: High-power attributes need value validation, not just escaping
cards.summary: Attributes like src and href can execute or load attacker-controlled content even when quotes are correctly escaped, so validate the URL itself.
cards.use_when: Any storefront flow that lets a user or merchant supply a URL for an image, link, iframe, or script — user avatars, custom collection banners, affiliate links, or rich-text product descriptions.
steps: Do not assume that escaping quotes is sufficient for src or href; even a well-contained value can cause a script to load or a page to navigate somewhere dangerous.
Validate that the supplied value is a well-formed, expected URL (correct scheme and shape) in addition to quoting and escaping it.
Explicitly reject the data: and javascript: schemes, which are legitimate URL forms but enable script execution and page injection.
For iframe or script sources specifically, restrict to trusted origins you control or explicitly allow.
When writing validation regexes, test them against data: and javascript: payloads, since these are easy to overlook and cause serious outcomes.
caveats: Data URLs have legitimate uses (see the data-URL card); the risk depends on where the value is inserted.
The source notes uncertainty about how some data-URL iframes are treated origin-wise; do not rely on iframe origin isolation without verifying.

cards.title: Reject data: and javascript: URLs in user-supplied links
cards.summary: data: and javascript: URLs can execute arbitrary code, so block them wherever users can supply a link or source.
cards.use_when: Building any feature that accepts a user-submitted link or image source — user-generated content, curated wishlists, third-party product feeds, or rich product description editors.
steps: Understand that a data: URL is a synthetic response from a non-existent server: the browser pretends to fetch it and treats the contents after the comma as the document.
Understand that a javascript: URL runs code in the current page; browsers such as Chrome may strip the javascript: prefix on paste, but users can re-add it, so do not rely on that.
Whitelist accepted schemes for user links (typically https) and reject everything else, rather than blacklisting only the two known-bad schemes.
For images, restrict to image data URLs or a controlled CDN origin if you must permit them at all.
Re-test after any change to link handling, and log rejected scheme attempts to spot abuse.
caveats: Chrome, Firefox and Safari handle pasted javascript: URLs differently (stripping the scheme or requiring a setting), so browser behaviour is not a reliable control.
Even if a data-URL iframe is isolated by origin, a heavy or blocking script inside it can still lock up the page in the shared event loop (a denial-of-service concern).

cards.title: Escaping alone fails inside inline event handlers and JS strings
cards.summary: When user data sits inside an inline handler (onclick) or a script string, you need JavaScript-level escaping in addition to HTML escaping, or break out is possible.
cards.use_when: Generating trigger text, analytics labels, or inline event handlers that embed store data, or embedding a user string inside a <script> variable.
steps: Recognise that data inside an onclick or script variable is in a JavaScript context nested inside an HTML context — one layer of escaping is not enough.
For strings inside JavaScript, escape quotes by prefixing with a backslash, and also escape backslashes themselves, otherwise a supplied backslash can neutralise your escape.
For values inserted into script variables, consider hex-encoding the data (using only 0-9 and A-F) so it cannot contain quotes, closing script tags or other breakout characters; decode it at runtime.
Alternatively use the HTML <template> tag as inert storage: put the escaped user data between tags (only < and & need escaping), then read it via JavaScript when needed.
Write tests with inputs containing quotes, backslashes, closing script tags and mixed contexts.
caveats: Pure HTML entity escaping inside a script produces garbage because the JavaScript parser has no concept of entities, so the user sees the wrong text.
The source notes some edge cases (e.g. double-backslash handling) were uncertain in the lecture — validate against your own parser and runtime.

cards.title: Avoid pages where user data passes through nested parsers
cards.summary: Layered contexts (HTML attribute to JavaScript string to eval-like call) require multiple correctly-ordered escapes and are extremely error-prone, so avoid the pattern.
cards.use_when: Designing features where store data flows through an HTML attribute, then a JavaScript string, then a dynamic execution call (e.g. rich-text widgets, custom button scripts, or analytics configuration).
steps: Identify nesting when a single value must be escaped at multiple levels — e.g. user data inside a string inside an onclick attribute, which the browser parses as HTML, then as JavaScript, then as a string argument.
Count the escapes required: each nested context adds its own layer, and getting the order or characters wrong breaks security.
Prefer architectures that avoid inline scripting and multi-layer embedding: pass data as escaped HTML between tags and read it via a script, rather than rebuilding scripts from strings.
If you cannot avoid nesting, write explicit tests that inject breakout characters at each layer and confirm nothing escapes.
Document the escaping contract wherever developers must remember multiple layers.
caveats: The source describes such nesting as surprisingly common in real code, but its recommended remedy is to avoid it rather than perfect the escaping.
No numeric guidance is given; the rule is architectural, not a formula.

cards.title: Only HTML element text and quoted attributes are reliably escapable
cards.summary: Several HTML contexts (comments, tag names, script bodies as plain text) cannot be escaped safely, so refuse to insert user data there.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or designing any template or editor where store or customer data could land in a comment, in a tag name, or directly in a script body.
steps: Refuse to insert user data into HTML comments — they do not affect rendering, so there is no legitimate need, and the parser rules are difficult to get right.
Refuse to build tag names from user input; even a blacklist of dangerous tags (script, style) will miss new tags and browser-specific interpretations.
Never place raw user data in an unquoted script position; use the hex-encoding or template-tag approaches described elsewhere.
Reserve the escapable contexts — ordinary element text and quoted attribute values — for any user-dependent content.
When a feature seems to require a non-escapable context, redesign the feature rather than attempting clever escaping.
caveats: The source states the comment-parsing rules were hard to pin down, which is itself a reason to avoid, not to improvise.
Blacklist approaches fail as browsers evolve and add new elements.

cards.title: Recognise reflected versus stored XSS and prioritise accordingly
cards.summary: Reflected XSS lives in the request, while stored XSS persists in your data and reaches every visitor regardless of the URL they use.
cards.use_when: Triageing vulnerability findings or designing storefront features: deciding where user data is stored (reviews, profiles, messages) versus only reflected in a response (search, filters).
steps: Classify a potential issue as reflected if the payload must be carried in a link the victim clicks (URL path or query).
Classify it as stored if the payload is persisted server-side — in a database, cache, or any durable field — and rendered for other visitors.
Treat stored issues as higher impact because the delivery route is irrelevant: the victim need not click anything from the attacker, so the whole user base is exposed.
Accept that the entry route for stored payloads can be obscure — an HTTP header, an API import, or a bribed insider — because any route to the data store suffices.
Prioritise fixes for stored flows: user profiles, uploaded content, review text, and anything that imports external data.
caveats: This is a classification framework, not a numeric severity scale; actual risk depends on the page and audience.
Stored XSS can be reached by means that would be impractical for reflected XSS, so do not use 'the attacker could not get them to click it' as a rejection reason.

cards.title: Escaping cannot defeat breakouts caused by a closing script tag
cards.summary: The HTML parser locates script tag boundaries before JavaScript parsing, so a literal closing script tag anywhere in a script breaks out regardless of string escaping.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any storefront or checkout page where user data or third-party content is embedded in a script, or when evaluating page-builder widgets that inject sequences into scripts.
steps: Understand the parser order: the HTML parser runs first and identifies script boundaries, then a separate JavaScript parser runs on each script body.

Recognise that including the literal characters for a closing script tag inside a string or comment in JavaScript still terminates the script element and can let an attacker resume HTML context, executing code.
Do not rely on escape sequences for quotes or backslashes to prevent this, because the boundary is determined before those sequences are interpreted.
Fix the embedding pattern: hex-encode the data so no breakout characters exist, or keep the data out of script bodies entirely.
Prefer loading third-party scripts by src from a trusted destination, which avoids this class of problem.
caveats: The source notes a syntax error in one script generally does not prevent other script elements from running, but the breakout itself is the security concern.
This applies wherever user data reaches a script body, including dynamically generated widgets.

cards.title: Blacklist filtering of tag names fails against forgiving HTML parsers
cards.summary: HTML parsers are deliberately lenient, accepting many syntax variations that bypass tag-name blacklists.
cards.use_when: Evaluating any input sanitisation that tries to block specific tags or words in customer reviews, product descriptions, or rich-text fields.
steps: Treat blacklists of tag names (script, style, etc.) as unreliable, because browsers accept unusual whitespace, slashes and other characters between a tag name and its attributes.
Assume new elements and browser-specific quirks will appear after your blacklist is written.
Where possible, work from an allowlist of the exact, minimal markup and attributes you intend to support, and escape everything else.
Understand the robustness principle ('be conservative in what you send, forgiving in what you accept') is why parsers are lenient — that leniency is a security liability for filters.
Validate changes against real browsers rather than assuming a filter behaves as written, and treat consistency across browsers as unproven.
caveats: The source notes older browsers differed significantly in how they interpreted unusual characters; modern behaviour is more consistent but still not safe to filter against.
This is a validation caution, not a recommendation to write your own full sanitiser.

cards.title: Beware DOM-injected globals via user-controlled element IDs
cards.summary: The DOM exposes elements with IDs as global JavaScript variables, so letting users choose an ID can let them inject or override variables your script depends on.
cards.use_when: Designing features that assign element IDs from user input, such as personalised widgets, review anchors, or per-customer page components.
steps: Recognise that the DOM creates a global JavaScript variable automatically for each element with an ID — this is a DOM behaviour, not a JavaScript feature.
If a script references a variable that is normally undefined and a user can set an element ID to that name, the condition can flip to truthy and divert the script's logic.
Do not let users control element IDs or form field names; generate IDs server-side from a safe pattern (e.g. a numeric token) instead.
Also avoid letting users control form field 'name' attributes, since forms rely on them.
When reviewing templates, treat any user-controlled identifier as a potential variable-injection point.
caveats: The source was uncertain how duplicate IDs are resolved, but notes duplicates can change which element JavaScript selects.
This is an indirect attack that depends on what your script does with the variable; not every case is exploitable.

cards.title: Use data URLs for small inline assets, not large ones
cards.summary: Data URLs can inline small images or stylesheets into a page to save an HTTP round trip, but they cannot be cached and bloat the document.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to inline small storefront assets such as icons or logos into the page or CSS, versus serving them as separate requests.
steps: Understand that an inlined data URL travels with the HTML or CSS, so the browser shows the asset on the first response instead of making an extra request, then waiting.
Inline only genuinely small assets; the source suggests a tiny icon may be worth it while a multi-megabyte image is not.
Recognise that inlined assets cannot be cached separately, so a large or repeat-viewed asset re-downloads with every page load.
Use the same technique inside CSS to avoid an extra HTTP request for small background images.
Weigh the round-trip saved against the added page weight before deciding.
caveats: The source gives no specific size threshold, only the principle that small is suitable and multi-megabyte is not.
Separately, data URLs are a security risk when users can supply them as link or source values — context determines whether they are helpful or dangerous.
